commands.desc: Connect to a fresh VPS as root
commands.tooltip: First contact with a new server: ssh (Secure Shell) logs in over the encrypted channel using the root account. The first prompt asks you to accept the server's host key (a fingerprint that identifies the machine) — verify it against the one shown in your provider's console. After login, run the update and upgrade steps below before installing anything.

commands.desc: Trust host key on first connection automatically
commands.tooltip: StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new records the server's host key into ~/.ssh/known_hosts the first time you connect without asking, but still refuses to connect if the key later changes. That stops man-in-the-middle attacks from day two onward. Use it in bootstrap scripts where a trust prompt would hang automation.

commands.cmd: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
commands.desc: Refresh package lists and upgrade all packages
commands.tooltip: The standard first step on any fresh VPS: apt update downloads the latest package lists, then apt upgrade -y installs every available update without prompting (the -y answers yes automatically). Run this before installing anything so security fixes and matching library versions are in place. Expect a reboot afterward if the kernel was updated.

commands.desc: Upgrade keeping existing config file versions
commands.tooltip: Forces apt to keep your current config files when a package upgrade wants to overwrite them: confdef keeps the default only if no local edit exists, confold always keeps your version. The -o flag injects dpkg options, so headless upgrades on production boxes never hang on interactive prompts. This is the safe variant when you have tuned configs you do not want clobbered.

commands.desc: Update package lists retrying flaky mirrors
commands.tooltip: Acquire::Retries=3 makes apt retry failed downloads up to three times, which tames the transient network errors common on new VPSes. A single dropped connection aborts the whole update run, so retries matter. Re-run your normal install command afterward if this still fails.

commands.cmd: sudo apt install -y ufw fail2ban unattended-upgrades curl htop
commands.desc: Install firewall, intrusion guard, and auto-updates
commands.tooltip: One-shot bootstrap install of the core hardening stack: ufw (the uncomplicated firewall), fail2ban (an auto-banning intrusion guard for brute-force attacks), unattended-upgrades (automatic security patches), plus curl and htop for diagnostics. Each ships with sane defaults so you can enable them one by one. This keeps the later setup steps to configuration only.

commands.cmd: sudo DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y ufw fail2ban unattended-upgrades curl htop
commands.desc: Install hardening stack without interactive prompts
commands.tooltip: DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive tells dpkg to skip all questions and use default answers, so the install never stalls waiting for input — the reliable form for bootstrap scripts and cloud-init user data. Add -o Dpkg::Options::="--force-confold" if you also want to protect existing config files. Combine with the retry option for flaky networks.

commands.desc: Install kernel headers for the running kernel
commands.tooltip: The $(uname -r) command substitution resolves to your exact kernel version, and linux-headers-<version> provides the build-time interfaces needed to compile DKMS drivers such as wireguard or GPU modules. Headers must match the running kernel exactly, which is why the substitution is used. Re-run after every kernel upgrade that needs modules rebuilt.

commands.desc: Install the btop system monitor
commands.tooltip: btop is a modern, GPU-accelerated resource monitor (htop's successor) showing CPU, memory, disks, network, and processes in one terminal screen. It is lighter than web dashboards and works over plain SSH. Navigate with the mouse or F-keys, and sort processes with P for CPU or M for memory.

commands.desc: Set the server clock to UTC
commands.tooltip: UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) is the VPS convention: it keeps log timestamps consistent across servers and regions, which matters when correlating failures. timedatectl is systemd's clock manager, and set-timezone persists across reboots. Confirm the result with timedatectl status.

commands.desc: Enable automatic security updates non-interactively
commands.tooltip: dpkg-reconfigure reruns a package's configuration step; for unattended-upgrades it flips on automatic security patching. The --frontend noninteractive flag answers its yes/no prompt with defaults so the command works in scripts. After this, the apt-daily-upgrade timer applies security updates nightly — check the log under /var/log/unattended-upgrades/.

commands.desc: Allow SSH through the firewall by app profile
commands.tooltip: OpenSSH is a ufw application profile (a named rule bundle) covering the port your SSH server listens on, normally 22/tcp. Allowing SSH first is the golden rule of firewall setup, because enabling ufw with no SSH rule locks you out of the box. Verify the profile's ports with ufw app info OpenSSH.

commands.cmd: sudo ufw allow proto tcp to any port 80,443 comment 'web traffic'
commands.desc: Allow HTTP and HTTPS on one rule with comment
commands.tooltip: One rule opens both web ports: the comma-separated list expands to 80 and 443, and proto tcp restricts it to TCP so UDP traffic stays blocked. The comment flag labels the rule for later audits and shows up in ufw status. Delete the whole list later with ufw delete followed by its number from ufw status numbered.

commands.cmd: sudo ufw limit 22/tcp comment 'SSH rate limit'
commands.desc: Rate-limit SSH connections to block brute force
commands.tooltip: limit applies ufw's rate limiter: connections are normally allowed, but an IP that opens 6 or more connections within 30 seconds is dropped, blunting brute-force password attacks without a full firewall ban. This is the firewall-level complement to fail2ban. The comment flag names the rule in ufw status output.

commands.desc: Delete firewall rule by its number
commands.tooltip: Deletes the rule shown as number 3 in ufw status numbered, the fastest way to remove a specific rule when several look identical. Always re-run ufw status numbered first, since numbers shift as rules change. Deleting by number removes only that one rule — the IPv6 twin of a dual-stack rule stays put.

commands.desc: Show ports opened by the OpenSSH app profile
commands.tooltip: Prints the definition of the OpenSSH application profile — the port and protocol it maps to — so you know exactly what ufw allow OpenSSH will open. Application profiles are the readable names ufw app list shows, letting you avoid remembering port numbers. Custom profiles live in /etc/ufw/applications.d/.

commands.desc: Insert a deny rule at the top of the list
commands.tooltip: insert 1 places the rule first, and that ordering matters because ufw evaluates rules in order and the first match wins — a top deny beats a later allow for the same traffic. This is the quick way to block a specific abusive IP without reordering everything. Verify the new order with ufw status numbered.

commands.desc: Preview a firewall rule without applying it
commands.tooltip: ufw --dry-run prints exactly what the rule would do — the underlying iptables commands — without changing anything, so you can sanity-check syntax before touching the live firewall. The same flag works with delete, insert, and enable. Run it as a rehearsal, then repeat without the flag.

commands.cmd: sudo ufw allow from 198.51.100.0/24 to any port 22 proto tcp comment 'office ssh'
commands.desc: Restrict SSH to an office IP range
commands.tooltip: Whitelists only the 198.51.100.0/24 subnet for SSH, so logins from anywhere else are refused at the firewall — stronger than rate limiting alone. The full-rule syntax adds from (source) and to (destination) with an optional comment. Combine with a deny-by-default incoming policy for a locked-down box.

commands.desc: Reject telnet port with a refusal response
commands.tooltip: Unlike deny, which silently drops packets, reject answers with a connection-refused response so the client fails fast instead of timing out — useful on ports you want to signal as closed. Port 23 (telnet) is plaintext and should be rejected or denied on any modern server. Note the distinction when diagnosing connectivity.

commands.desc: Back up sshd config with today's date suffix
commands.tooltip: Snapshots the SSH daemon config before you edit it: $(date +%F) expands to today's date (YYYY-MM-DD), so the backup file keeps a recognizable timestamp. If a hardening edit locks you out, restore by copying the backup back over sshd_config. Keep the backup until the new config has survived a restart.

commands.desc: Disable root login over SSH
commands.tooltip: sed edits the file in place (-i): the pattern ^#PermitRootLogin.* matches the commented-out default line and rewrites it as PermitRootLogin no, which refuses direct root logins. Admins then use a normal user plus sudo instead, so brute-forcing root becomes pointless. Run sudo sshd -t and restart ssh afterward.

commands.desc: Enable SSH public key authentication
commands.tooltip: Uncomments PubkeyAuthentication to yes, allowing login with a key pair — a private key you hold and a public key stored in the account's authorized_keys file. Keys are the recommended SSH credential because they cannot be guessed like passwords. This is the prerequisite before disabling password auth.

commands.desc: Disable SSH password authentication (lockout risk)
commands.tooltip: WARNING — this command can lock you out: it turns off password logins, so only key-based access works. Apply it only after testing that your key logs in successfully, and never close the current SSH session until you have confirmed reconnection. Also check /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf for a PasswordAuthentication line, since those fragments override this file.

commands.desc: Test sshd config syntax before restarting
commands.tooltip: sshd -t parses the configuration and reports errors without touching the running daemon — the mandatory safety check after any sshd_config edit. The -f flag names the config file to test explicitly. If it prints nothing, the config is valid and safe to apply with sudo systemctl restart ssh.

commands.desc: Show effective SSH auth settings after overrides
commands.tooltip: sshd -T dumps the effective configuration the daemon would actually use, merging the main file and all drop-in fragments under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/. Grepping the three auth directives confirms what the server will really enforce — essential because later files can override earlier ones. Compare this output with your intended settings.

commands.desc: Restart the SSH daemon to apply config
commands.tooltip: Applies sshd_config changes by restarting the ssh service (Ubuntu's unit name is ssh; Debian uses sshd — either works via alias). Only restart after sudo sshd -t passes, because a bad config can kill the daemon and lock you out. Do not close your current session until a fresh login succeeds.

commands.desc: Check SSH daemon status and recent log lines
commands.tooltip: Shows whether the ssh service is running, enabled at boot, and its most recent log entries; --no-pager prints directly instead of opening a pager, which matters over SSH where pagers can hang. A green 'active (running)' line plus 'Loaded: enabled' is the healthy state. Use is-active for a script-friendly yes/no answer.

commands.desc: Report whether SSH service is running
commands.tooltip: Prints a single word — active, inactive, or failed — that scripts can parse, unlike the verbose status output. is-active checks only the current state, while is-enabled asks whether the unit starts at boot. Both exit non-zero when the answer is no, which makes them natural if conditions in shell scripts.

commands.desc: Check whether SSH starts at boot
commands.tooltip: Prints enabled, disabled, or static — the boot-time policy for the ssh service rather than its current state. On fresh VPSes ssh should already be enabled, but a minimal image may disable it. Pair with sudo systemctl enable ssh if the answer is disabled.

commands.desc: Test that key-only SSH login works
commands.tooltip: Forces the client to attempt only key authentication: if your key is set up the login succeeds, and if the server would need a password the attempt fails fast instead of prompting. This is the safe pre-flight test before disabling password auth server-side. A successful exit means the server is ready for hardening.

commands.desc: Connect with explicit port and identity key
commands.tooltip: Logs in as deploy using the private key at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (the -i flag selects the identity file) and the explicit -p 22 port. Being explicit sidesteps surprises from ~/.ssh/config aliases or non-standard ports. The matching public key must be listed in the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

commands.desc: Keep idle SSH sessions alive with pings
commands.tooltip: ServerAliveInterval=60 makes the client send a keepalive every 60 seconds, so NAT gateways and firewalls that drop idle connections won't silently kill your session — common during long deploys and tail -f monitoring. The server-side counterpart is ClientAliveInterval. Without it, a quiet session can freeze and only respond after a long timeout.

commands.desc: Forward SSH agent for key chaining (caution)
commands.tooltip: WARNING — agent forwarding (-A) lets the remote host use your local SSH agent to authenticate onward, which is convenient for git pulls from the server but hands your key to anyone who compromises it. Prefer ssh -J (ProxyJump) or a dedicated deploy key instead. Only enable it transiently on trusted hosts.

commands.desc: Jump through a bastion host to reach the server
commands.tooltip: ProxyJump (-J) chains connections: it opens an SSH session to bastion.example.com and tunnels through it to the destination, so the target only ever sees the bastion's IP. This is the standard way to reach servers on private networks without agent forwarding. Multiple jumps can be comma-separated.

commands.cmd: ssh -t deploy@203.0.113.10 sudo systemctl status nginx
commands.desc: Run sudo remotely with a forced pseudo-terminal
commands.tooltip: The -t flag allocates a pseudo-terminal, which sudo requires when prompting for a password — without it you get 'sudo: no tty present'. This runs one command on the server and returns, the building block of remote administration. Add -tt if even the sudo prompt needs a TTY.

commands.desc: Dump the effective SSH client configuration
commands.tooltip: ssh -G prints the resolved client configuration for the given host — which hostname, port, identity files, and options would actually be used — without connecting. It is the debugger for mysterious ssh behavior caused by ~/.ssh/config rules. Pipe to grep to inspect specific settings.

commands.desc: Pre-record a host key into known_hosts
commands.tooltip: ssh-keyscan fetches the server's public host keys and appends them to known_hosts, pre-answering the first-connection trust prompt — handy in provisioning scripts that run non-interactively. The -t ed25519 flag limits the scan to that key type. Since it trusts without verification, compare the key against your provider's console fingerprint.

commands.desc: Copy a file to the server over SSH
commands.tooltip: scp (secure copy) transfers files inside an SSH connection; note the uppercase -P for the port, unlike ssh's lowercase -p, and -i selects the identity key. The destination is user@host:/path. This is the manual deploy step — a tar of your app or a config file — that scripts later replace with rsync or git.

commands.desc: Create a deploy user for key-only login
commands.tooltip: Adds a deploy account with no password (--disabled-password) and an empty comment field (--gecos ''), so it can only be reached with an SSH key — the safest shape for an app-deploying service account. Add the key with mkdir -p /home/deploy/.ssh and echo into authorized_keys. Grant sudo separately with usermod -aG sudo.

commands.desc: Restrict SSH logins to named users only
commands.tooltip: AllowUsers whitelists which accounts may log in over SSH — here only deploy — so every other user (including root) is refused even with a valid key. It is defense in depth after PermitRootLogin no. Keep the setting commented out on hosts where LDAP or other tools manage access.

commands.desc: Limit SSH authentication attempts to three
commands.tooltip: MaxAuthTries 3 cuts the number of failed auth attempts before the connection is dropped, slowing brute-force guessing at the daemon level (fail2ban handles repeat offenders at the firewall). Each attempt can also be a key offer, so generous key agents can hit the limit. Re-test after applying.

commands.desc: Drop SSH connections idle for five minutes
commands.tooltip: ClientAliveInterval 300 makes the server send keepalives every 300 seconds and disconnect clients that never answer — cleaning up abandoned sessions that otherwise hold connections and processes. This is the server-side counterpart to the client's ServerAliveInterval. Choose a value larger than your slowest legitimate operation.

commands.desc: Tunnel a remote port with fail-fast forwarding
commands.tooltip: Local forwarding (-L 3000:localhost:3000) exposes the server's port 3000 on your machine's port 3000, as if the app ran locally — the classic way to reach admin UIs bound to localhost. ExitOnForwardFailure=yes aborts the session if the forward cannot be established instead of silently continuing. The left port is local; the right side resolves on the server.

commands.desc: List public keys currently loaded in the agent
commands.tooltip: Prints the public keys your SSH agent holds, which is what gets offered to servers when authenticating (and forwarded with -A). If a server keeps asking for a passphrase, the key is probably not loaded — add it with ssh-add. The -l variant shows fingerprints instead of full keys.

commands.desc: Edit the SSH client config file
commands.tooltip: ~/.ssh/config defines per-host shortcuts and options: Host aliases, IdentityFile paths, ProxyJump chains, and default ports, so a plain 'ssh web' expands to a full connection recipe. Settings here are the client-side mirror of the server hardening you just did. Keep permissions at 600 — the file may reference private keys.

commands.desc: Restart the fail2ban server
commands.tooltip: fail2ban-client is the control socket for the fail2ban-server daemon, and restart re-runs it, re-reading all jails (per-service ban configurations) from disk. Use it after editing jail.local when a plain reload is not enough. Bans tracked only in memory are lost; the persistent database survives.

commands.desc: Change failed-attempt threshold for sshd jail
commands.tooltip: set <jail> <variable> <value> tunes a running jail without editing files: maxretry 5 means five matching failures within the findtime window trigger a ban. Changes apply immediately but revert on restart unless mirrored in jail.local. This is the live-tuning counterpart to editing the config.

commands.desc: Set the ban trigger window to ten minutes
commands.tooltip: findtime is the sliding window in seconds over which failures are counted — 600 means the maxretry failures must happen within ten minutes to earn a ban. Longer windows catch slow scanners, shorter ones avoid false positives from your own typos. The value applies to the running jail only.

commands.desc: Whitelist an IP for the sshd jail
commands.tooltip: addignoreip exempts an address from bans for that jail — essential for your own office IP, which might otherwise trip the threshold during maintenance. 192.0.2.10 is the documentation-range stand-in for your real address. Remove the exemption with the matching delignoreip command.

commands.desc: Remove an IP from the sshd ignore list
commands.tooltip: Undoes a previous addignoreip, so the address becomes eligible for banning again. Useful when an IP that was whitelisted for maintenance should no longer be trusted. Verify the current ignore list via sudo fail2ban-client status sshd.

commands.desc: Read the current maxretry value for sshd
commands.tooltip: get <jail> <variable> queries the running jail's effective settings — useful to confirm a live set command took effect before it is lost on restart. The value shown is what the daemon is enforcing right now, which may differ from jail.local if you tuned it live. Other readable variables include findtime and bantime.

commands.cmd: sudo fail2ban-client status sshd | grep -E 'Currently banned|Banned IP list'
commands.desc: Show only the banned IPs for the sshd jail
commands.tooltip: Filters the verbose status output down to the two lines that matter: how many IPs are banned right now and which addresses they are. If the list shows your own IP, you tripped the threshold and need unbanip. This is the first command to run when diagnosing an unreachable server.

commands.desc: List which fail2ban jails are active
commands.tooltip: The plain status command prints one summary block per jail plus a 'Jail list:' line naming every enabled jail (sshd, nginx-http-auth, and so on). Grepping for that line gives a compact overview of what fail2ban is actually protecting. A jail missing from the list means its config did not load.

commands.desc: Manually ban an IP in the sshd jail
commands.tooltip: Instantly bans the address without waiting for it to trip the failure threshold — the right move when you spot an attacker in the logs. The ban is applied through the jail's firewall action, so it behaves like an automatic ban. Lift it with the matching unbanip when the threat is over.

commands.desc: Manually unban an IP in the sshd jail
commands.tooltip: Removes an existing ban immediately, whether it was set manually or automatically — the fix when a legitimate user gets locked out by too many failed attempts. Use get sshd banned to confirm the address was banned before issuing this. The ban returns if the offending behavior continues.

commands.desc: Show a compact banned-IP summary for sshd
commands.tooltip: The short flavor (a positional argument, not a flag) condenses the jail status into just the banned count and IP list, made for quick eyeballing and scripts. Newer fail2ban versions also support basic, cymru, and stats flavors. This is the lightest way to poll ban state in a monitoring loop.

commands.desc: Show fail2ban ban statistics table
commands.tooltip: Prints a table of statistics across all jails — matches, bans, and other counters that reveal whether the intrusion guard is actually catching anything. A jail with zero bans after weeks of uptime may have a broken filter or log path. Reset the counters by restarting the fail2ban server.

commands.desc: Follow fail2ban log live
commands.tooltip: Streams new log lines as they are written, showing bans, unbans, and jail actions in real time — the way to watch an attack unfold or debug a jail that never triggers. tail -f (follow) keeps the file open; Ctrl-C stops it. The log is also the first place to look when fail2ban silently does nothing.

commands.desc: Show ban tuning values from jail.local
commands.tooltip: jail.local is the override file where local fail2ban settings belong (jail.conf holds the shipped defaults). This grep pulls the three tuning knobs — bantime (ban duration), findtime (counting window), maxretry (failure threshold) — so you can see the effective policy at a glance. Values here override the defaults in jail.conf.

commands.desc: Start fail2ban and enable it at boot
commands.tooltip: enable --now combines two steps: it registers the service to start automatically at boot (enable) and starts it immediately (now). Fail2ban only protects what is running, so a server that reboots without this enabled loses its ban behavior entirely. Confirm with sudo fail2ban-client status.

commands.desc: Reload fail2ban config without dropping bans
commands.tooltip: Signals the service to re-read its configuration through fail2ban-client reload, applying jail changes while keeping current bans and the daemon running — gentler than restart. Use this after editing jail.local when you don't want to lose in-memory state. Deeper config changes may still need a full restart.

commands.desc: Run automatic security upgrades now
commands.tooltip: unattended-upgrade (singular binary) applies the security and allowed-origin updates configured in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades right now, outside its normal nightly schedule. It resolves dependencies and handles dpkg config-file prompts automatically. Output lands in /var/log/unattended-upgrades/unattended-upgrades.log.

commands.desc: Simulate automatic upgrades without applying
commands.tooltip: The --dry-run flag simulates the whole upgrade pass and prints what would be installed without changing anything — the safe way to test new Allowed-Origins entries before trusting them to run unattended. Nothing is downloaded and nothing is modified. Run this after editing 50unattended-upgrades.

commands.desc: Run automatic upgrades with debug logging
commands.tooltip: The -d flag (short for --debug) repeats the upgrade with extra diagnostic detail written to the log — including why specific packages were skipped, which is the first thing to check when updates silently don't happen. It is debugging output, not a dry run: real updates are applied. Use --dry-run when you want a simulation instead.

commands.desc: Find the auto-reboot settings in the config
commands.tooltip: grep -n prints matching lines with their line numbers so you can jump straight to the Automatic-Reboot options (which control whether the server reboots itself after kernel updates) in the 50unattended-upgrades config file. Most lines there ship commented out — uncomment and set to true only if you accept unattended reboots. The line numbers make the follow-up edit trivial.

commands.desc: Edit the unattended-upgrades policy file
commands.tooltip: This is the master config for automatic updates: Allowed-Origins lists which package origins may install themselves (security by default), and Automatic-Reboot governs post-update reboots. Changes apply on the next run, no restart needed. Commented lines are examples — uncomment the section you actually want.

commands.desc: Read the tail of the auto-update log
commands.tooltip: Shows the last 30 lines of the log where every automatic run records its decisions — packages upgraded, skipped, or held back. The final line usually reports when the next run is scheduled. If your server hasn't updated in weeks, this log shows why.

commands.desc: Check the auto-update service status
commands.tooltip: unattended-upgrades runs as a one-shot systemd service that applies updates when triggered by the apt-daily-upgrade timer. Status shows whether recent runs succeeded and any error output. A failed unit explains missing security patches; restart it and re-check the log.

commands.desc: Restart the auto-update service
commands.tooltip: Re-runs the one-shot service immediately, the nudge to apply pending updates without waiting for the timer — useful after editing 50unattended-upgrades or when a previous run died mid-way. The service exits once the update pass completes. Log output goes to the usual unattended-upgrades log.

commands.desc: Check when automatic updates are scheduled
commands.tooltip: apt-daily-upgrade.timer is the systemd timer that wakes the unattended-upgrades service on a randomized daily schedule — the random offset keeps thousands of servers from hitting mirrors at once. Status shows the next trigger time and the countdown. If the timer is inactive, nothing updates automatically.

commands.desc: Pause automatic updates (undo with unmask)
commands.tooltip: WARNING — this stops automatic security patching: mask makes the timer unstartable by anything, including other units that try to pull it in, so no updates apply until you unmask. It is the deliberate choice for maintenance windows or fully manual update policies. Re-enable with sudo systemctl unmask apt-daily-upgrade.timer.

commands.desc: Restore the automatic update timer
commands.tooltip: Removes the mask so apt-daily-upgrade.timer can run again and automatic security updates resume. The timer still honors its randomized daily schedule — run sudo systemctl start apt-daily-upgrade.timer if you want it immediately. Confirm the change with sudo systemctl list-timers.

commands.desc: List upgradable packages without the header
commands.tooltip: apt list --upgradable prints every package with a newer version available; the grep -v '^Listing' strips the informational first line, leaving clean package:version output. This is the pre-upgrade reconnaissance step. Pipe to wc -l for a simple count of pending updates.

commands.desc: Count pending upgrades without applying
commands.tooltip: apt-get -s (simulate) computes the upgrade and prints one Inst line per package to be installed; grep -c counts them. The result is the number of pending updates — ideal for monitoring scripts and deciding when to schedule a maintenance reboot. Nothing is downloaded or changed.

commands.desc: Upgrade the server to the next release (caution)
commands.tooltip: WARNING — this performs a major OS release upgrade (for example Ubuntu 22.04 to 24.04) with reboots and service interruptions, and it can take a long time over SSH. Always snapshot the VPS or take a full backup first, and keep the session alive — a dropped connection mid-upgrade is painful. Run it from a screen or tmux session.

commands.desc: Upgrade with new dependencies and removals
commands.tooltip: dist-upgrade is a smarter upgrade: it installs new dependencies and removes conflicting packages when needed, going beyond plain upgrade's conservative policy. That makes it slightly riskier on production boxes — it can remove packages you use. On Debian-based systems it is how kernel and library transitions get applied.

commands.desc: Reboot the server immediately
commands.tooltip: shutdown -r now schedules an immediate reboot, gracefully stopping services first — the polite form after kernel or library upgrades. The now argument skips the default one-minute warning; use shutdown -r +5 to delay. Always verify services come back with sudo systemctl status or uptime afterward.

commands.desc: Install the upgrade changelog viewer
commands.tooltip: apt-listchanges intercepts apt operations and shows the changelog of packages being upgraded, so unattended and manual updates stop being a mystery. It runs in non-interactive mode for unattended-upgrades and can display or email summaries. This is the standard companion that makes auto-updates auditable.

commands.desc: Create a 2GB swap file (size first)
commands.tooltip: fallocate instantly reserves a 2G file for swap — disk-backed memory overflow — without writing zeros, which makes it faster than dd. The file must then be secured (chmod 600), formatted (mkswap), and activated (swapon). On filesystems without fallocate support, use dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=2048 instead.

commands.desc: Restrict swap file permissions to root
commands.tooltip: Swap files contain memory pages, so they must not be world-readable — 600 grants read/write only to root. Both mkswap and swapon warn or refuse on a too-permissive swapfile. Run this immediately after creating the file and before formatting it.

commands.desc: Format the file as swap space
commands.tooltip: mkswap writes a swap filesystem signature into the file — the formatting step that turns a plain file into usable swap. WARNING: the command erases whatever the target previously contained, so point it only at your fresh swapfile. After this, swapon activates it and swapon --show confirms the size.

commands.desc: Activate the swap file now
commands.tooltip: swapon enables the swap file for the current session, so the kernel can page memory out to it immediately. This is step four of the swap sequence (fallocate, chmod 600, mkswap, swapon). Activation does not survive reboot until you add a line to /etc/fstab.

commands.desc: Deactivate swap before resizing or removal
commands.tooltip: swapoff moves swapped-out pages back into RAM and disables the swap file — the required prelude to resizing or deleting it. WARNING: if RAM is full, this can stall or OOM-kill processes, so do it when memory is comfortable. Afterward you can safely delete the file and recreate it larger.

commands.desc: Persist a low swappiness setting
commands.tooltip: Appends vm.swappiness=10 to /etc/sysctl.conf so the kernel keeps a calm 10% preference for swap (swappiness is the 0-100 eagerness to swap; servers often prefer 10 over the default 60). tee -a writes the echoed line with root privileges, appending without touching existing content. The value takes effect after sudo sysctl --system or a reboot.

commands.desc: Set swappiness immediately without reboot
commands.tooltip: The -w flag writes a kernel parameter live: vm.swappiness=10 tells the kernel to prefer RAM and swap less aggressively, which helps latency-sensitive services. This change is temporary — it resets on reboot unless persisted in /etc/sysctl.conf. Check the current value with cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness.

commands.desc: Reload all sysctl settings from files
commands.tooltip: Re-reads every file in the sysctl configuration tree (/etc/sysctl.conf plus /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf) and applies the settings — how you activate persisted tunables without rebooting. Later files override earlier ones in the read order. Run this after appending to sysctl.conf to confirm your values took.

commands.desc: Clone the app repository to the server
commands.tooltip: Copies the example/myapp repository from GitHub into /opt/myapp (the conventional location for self-contained server applications) over HTTPS. The clone contains the full history, enabling clean pull-based deploys afterward. For private repos, use an SSH remote or a deploy token instead of interactive credentials.

commands.desc: Create app directory owned by the deploy user
commands.tooltip: mkdir -p creates /opt/myapp (and parents, if missing), then chown hands ownership to the deploy account so that user can write, build, and pull without sudo. Keeping the service user as owner avoids running the app as root. If the directory already existed, only the ownership changes.

commands.desc: Install production npm dependencies cleanly
commands.tooltip: npm ci installs dependencies exactly from package-lock.json (the pinned dependency manifest), wiping node_modules first — the reproducible, CI-grade install for deploys. --omit=dev skips development packages, shrinking the footprint and the attack surface. The cd first positions you in the app directory; every later deploy step runs from here.

commands.cmd: sudo -u deploy bash -lc 'cd /opt/myapp && npm ci --omit=dev && npm run build'
commands.desc: Install deps and build as the deploy user
commands.tooltip: Runs the install-and-build pipeline as the deploy user via sudo -u, with bash -lc giving it a login shell so PATH and nvm settings apply. The single-quoted chain does a clean npm ci, then npm run build for compiled frontends. Building as a non-root user keeps the artifacts owned by deploy, not root.

commands.desc: Start the app service and enable it at boot
commands.tooltip: enable --now registers myapp.service to start on boot and launches it immediately — the one command that turns a fresh systemd unit (defined in /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service) into a running, reboot-safe service. The .service suffix is optional but explicit. Confirm with sudo systemctl status myapp.

commands.desc: Restart the app service to apply a deploy
commands.tooltip: The core deploy step: restarts the systemd unit so it loads the newly pulled code, rebuilt assets, or edited environment. systemd stops the old process, starts the new one, and reports failure if the unit cannot come up. For zero-downtime patterns prefer an ExecReload or a rolling restart.

commands.desc: Inspect app service state with full log lines
commands.tooltip: Shows the unit's current state, uptime, and recent log output; -l disables line truncation and --no-pager prints directly — both matter when debugging a crash over SSH. 'Active: active (running)' plus a recent Main PID is the healthy signature. This is the first stop after every deploy.

commands.desc: Clear a crashed service's failed state
commands.tooltip: After too many quick restarts, systemd marks a unit as 'failed' and refuses to start it until reset — reset-failed clears that state so you can retry. It does not fix the underlying crash, but it unblocks the restart loop during debugging. The unit reverts to failed again if the next start also dies.

commands.desc: Print the service unit file in full
commands.tooltip: Shows the complete unit definition — ExecStart command, user, environment, restart policy — exactly as systemd loaded it, including any drop-in overrides from systemctl edit. This is the fastest way to answer 'what is this service actually running?'. It only reads, so it is safe to run anytime.

commands.desc: Show the service's main process ID
commands.tooltip: systemctl show exposes machine-readable unit properties; -p MainPID filters to just the process ID of the service's main process. That PID is what you target with ps, strace, or kill when investigating a specific worker. A value of 0 means the service is not currently running.

commands.desc: Follow the app's logs live
commands.tooltip: journalctl -u filters the systemd journal (the binary log store) to one unit, and -f follows new lines as they appear — the standard 'watch the deploy roll out' command. Every stdout/stderr line the service writes lands here. Ctrl-C stops following; the filter also applies to plain reads, so you can scroll back.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 app log lines
commands.tooltip: Prints the newest 100 journal entries for the unit (the -n count, short for --lines) without opening a pager, which is the first diagnostic after a crash or failed deploy. Because the journal is ordered newest-last, this is the tail of the app's story. Add --since '30 min ago' to narrow the window.

commands.desc: Show today's app warnings and errors
commands.tooltip: Combines two filters: --since today limits the window to the current day, and -p warning keeps only entries at warning priority or higher, hiding routine info chatter. The result is a short list of things that actually need attention after a deploy. Raise to -p err for errors only.

commands.cmd: sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
commands.desc: Validate nginx config then reload it
commands.tooltip: The safe config-change ritual: nginx -t tests the syntax first, and only if it passes (the && short-circuit) does systemctl reload apply it — reload gracefully restarts workers without dropping connections. If the test fails, nothing changes and your current config stays live. Never reload on a failing test.

commands.desc: Install nginx web server
commands.tooltip: Installs the nginx reverse proxy and static file server that fronts your app on ports 80 and 443 in the classic VPS layout. The -y flag answers the install prompt automatically. After install, the service starts and is enabled by default on Ubuntu; your site config goes in /etc/nginx/sites-available/.

commands.cmd: cd /opt/myapp && git pull --ff-only origin main && sudo systemctl restart myapp
commands.desc: Pull latest code and restart the service
commands.tooltip: The minimal deploy loop: fast-forward pull the main branch (--ff-only refuses merges, so a diverged local tree fails loudly instead of creating a mess), then restart the systemd unit to load the new code. In one line it updates, verifies, and applies. For compiled apps, add the build step between pull and restart.

commands.cmd: sudo -u deploy git -C /opt/myapp pull origin main
commands.desc: Pull latest code as the deploy user
commands.tooltip: git -C runs the command in the given directory without a cd; sudo -u deploy runs it as the deploy user, who owns the checkout — necessary when the repo was cloned by that account and root would otherwise hit ownership errors. A clean pull here means the working tree matched, keeping deploy state predictable.

commands.desc: Show the deployed commit hash
commands.tooltip: Prints the abbreviated commit SHA currently checked out in /opt/myapp — the exact code version running in production. Compare it with your CI's latest build to prove a deploy actually landed. The full hash (drop --short) is what you would record in a deployment log.

commands.desc: Show the last five commits on the server
commands.tooltip: Lists the five most recent commits in the deployed checkout, one per line, giving a quick sense of how far behind (or ahead) production is. Each line is the short hash plus the commit subject. Combined with rev-parse, this turns git into a poor man's deployment history.

commands.cmd: ssh deploy@203.0.113.10 'cd /opt/myapp && git pull && sudo systemctl restart myapp'
commands.desc: Deploy remotely in a single SSH command
commands.tooltip: Runs the whole update-and-restart sequence on the server without an interactive shell: ssh executes the quoted command list remotely and returns its exit status. Quoting matters — the remote shell must see the && chain intact. This one-liner is the seed of every deploy script that follows.

commands.cmd: sudo systemctl restart myapp && sleep 3 && curl -sf http://localhost:3000/health && echo DEPLOY_OK
commands.desc: Restart app and verify health endpoint
commands.tooltip: The deploy acceptance test: restart the service, wait 3 seconds for startup, then curl the health endpoint with -sf (silent, fail on error) so a non-200 response aborts the chain — DEPLOY_OK prints only when the app is genuinely up. Extend the sleep for slower boots. This turns 'it restarted' into 'it works'.

commands.desc: Create the web root for a site
commands.tooltip: mkdir -p creates the document root for example.com, including any missing parent directories — the standard location nginx serves static files from. The -p flag makes the command idempotent: it succeeds even if the directory already exists. Ownership typically moves to www-data next.

commands.desc: Give the web server ownership of the site
commands.tooltip: chown -R recursively hands /var/www/example.com to www-data, the user nginx workers run as, so the server can read (and if configured, write) the site files. Files owned by root would still be readable if permissions allow, but www-data ownership is the convention. Use -R with care on trees containing secrets.

commands.desc: Verify the site answers with HTTP 200
commands.tooltip: curl -I sends a HEAD request (headers only), and the grep filters for the HTTP status line — the quick post-deploy proof that nginx, the app, and the certificate all answer. 200 means the site is live; 502 or 503 points at the app behind the proxy. Use -k to test before the certificate is valid.

commands.desc: Audit all virtual hosts in one pass
commands.tooltip: nginx -T dumps every loaded config file as one merged document, and the grep pulls out the server_name (hostname) and listen (port) lines — a full map of what the server answers for. It reveals overlapping server blocks that can cause traffic to hit the wrong site. This is the config-level site inventory.

commands.cmd: sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart myapp
commands.desc: Reload unit definitions then restart the app
commands.tooltip: After editing a service file, daemon-reload tells systemd to re-read unit definitions — restart alone would use the stale version. Chaining them applies new ExecStart lines, environment variables, or resource limits, then restarts the app under the new unit. Run the reload first or the restart silently keeps old settings.

commands.desc: Renew a single named certificate
commands.tooltip: certbot renew normally processes every certificate on the box; --cert-name example.com narrows it to one, selected by the name shown in certbot certificates. It still respects the 30-day renewal window — nothing happens if the certificate is not close to expiring. This is the targeted form for per-site renewal scripts.

commands.desc: Renew silently and reload nginx on success
commands.tooltip: The cron-friendly form: --quiet suppresses all output except errors, and --deploy-hook runs the quoted command only when a certificate was actually renewed — the hook makes nginx pick up the new certificate files. Because it runs only on real renewal, it is safe on a nightly schedule. This mirrors what the packaged certbot timer does.

commands.cmd: sudo certbot renew --standalone --pre-hook 'systemctl stop nginx' --post-hook 'systemctl start nginx'
commands.desc: Renew with a standalone server and service hooks
commands.tooltip: For renewals when nginx holds port 80: --standalone makes certbot run its own temporary web server on port 80 to answer the challenge, so nginx must be stopped first (--pre-hook) and started again after (--post-hook). The pre/post hooks bracket the whole run. Expect a brief downtime during the swap.

commands.desc: Schedule nightly certbot renewal via cron
commands.tooltip: A crontab line: at 03:15 daily, run certbot renew quietly and reload nginx only when a renewal actually happens (the --quiet and --deploy-hook pattern from the Certbot docs). The five fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. Note that the packaged certbot.timer already does this on Ubuntu — add this only if you manage cron yourself.

commands.cmd: sudo certbot certonly --nginx --cert-name example.com -d example.com -d www.example.com
commands.desc: Issue a cert for two domains under one name
commands.tooltip: certonly obtains certificates without touching nginx site config — the --nginx flag only handles the ACME challenge, while the -d flags list every domain to cover (example.com and www.example.com become SAN, subject-alternative-name entries). --cert-name gives the bundle a stable name for later renew --cert-name calls. Renewal continues automatically via the timer.

commands.cmd: sudo certbot certificates | grep -E 'Certificate Name|Expiry Date'
commands.desc: List certificate names and expiry dates
commands.tooltip: Filters certbot certificates down to the two lines that matter per certificate: the name and the expiration date. Scanning this output tells you at a glance whether any certificate is creeping toward its 30-day renewal window. Pair with a calendar reminder for manual review.

commands.desc: Change a certificate's renewal options
commands.tooltip: reconfigure rewrites how one certificate is renewed — webroot path, plugins, hooks — using the options you pass, then validates the change with a test renewal against the staging server before saving. It is the supported way to fix a certificate whose renewal method changed (say, nginx to webroot). See certbot certificates for valid names.

commands.desc: Edit the root user's crontab
commands.tooltip: Opens root's cron table (the crontab) in the default editor — the place for system-level jobs like nightly renewals, backups, and cleanup scripts that need privileges. Each line is a schedule plus a command. Jobs here run as root, so review them with the care root deserves.

commands.desc: List the root user's scheduled jobs
commands.tooltip: Prints every cron job scheduled for root, one per line, with the five time fields followed by the command. This is the audit command when you inherit a server: you see at a glance what runs automatically. Compare it against your mental model of the server's maintenance.

commands.desc: Show cron jobs excluding comments
commands.tooltip: The pipe strips blank and comment lines (those starting with #) from the crontab output, leaving only active job lines — the clean view for auditing. Commented lines are disabled jobs, so the filtered list is what actually executes. Add -w to also skip whitespace-only lines if you prefer.

commands.desc: Show scheduled maintenance timers
commands.tooltip: list-timers --all shows every systemd timer with its next run time and the unit it triggers; grepping for apt, unattended, and certbot surfaces exactly the maintenance schedule — automatic updates and certificate renewals. If a timer is missing here, that maintenance silently isn't happening. Timers are systemd's modern replacement for cron.

commands.desc: Snapshot server configs before changes
commands.tooltip: Bundles the SSH, firewall, and fail2ban config trees into one compressed archive (czf = create, gzip, file) named with today's date via $(date +%F). Restoring is a tar -xzf of the same file. A five-second backup before a hardening session turns a mistake into a one-command rollback.

commands.desc: Show errors from the previous boot
commands.tooltip: journalctl -b -1 addresses the boot before the current one (-b alone is the current boot, -b -1 the previous), and -p err filters to errors and above. This is the first stop when a server came back unhealthy after a reboot: it shows what went wrong during the previous session. Combine with -u myapp to scope it to one service.

commands.desc: Show SSH brute-force attempts from the journal
commands.tooltip: Filters the SSH service's current-boot journal entries for failed password lines, revealing how much password guessing the box is absorbing — the justification for key-only auth and fail2ban. The journal often holds lines that log rotation has already purged from /var/log/auth.log. Pair with wc -l for a count.

commands.desc: Show the last ten successful key logins
commands.tooltip: Every successful key-based SSH login writes an Accepted publickey line to auth.log; this shows the ten most recent, with user, source IP, and key fingerprint. It is the audit trail for 'who actually logged in' — compare it with your expectations after an incident. For password logins, grep Accepted password instead.

commands.desc: List server shutdown and reboot history
commands.tooltip: The last command reads the wtmp log of login sessions; -x includes system events, and filtering by the shutdown and reboot record types shows the box's restart history with timestamps. An unexpected reboot pattern here hints at crashes, kernel panics, or OOM-triggered resets. Check dmesg for the cause.

commands.desc: Confirm SSH is listening on port 22
commands.tooltip: ss -tlnp lists listening (-l) TCP (-t) sockets with process names (-p, hence sudo); grepping for :22 confirms sshd bound to the port after a restart. The output includes the listening address and the owning process — the same check applies to any port when diagnosing 'can't connect'. Compare with ss -tlnp | grep :443 for the web stack.

commands.desc: Remove orphaned packages and their configs
commands.tooltip: autoremove deletes packages that became unneeded after upgrades or removals (dangling dependencies), and --purge also deletes their config files — a periodic hygiene step that frees disk and reduces attack surface. The -y flag skips the confirmation. It never touches explicitly installed packages, so it is safe after deploys.

commands.desc: Find the largest log files
commands.tooltip: du -sh reports each log's total size in human units; sort -rh orders by size descending; head -10 keeps the top ten. A log that has grown to gigabytes is usually a chatty service or a broken rotation — the fix is usually logrotate config. This is disk-forensics 101 on a full server.

commands.desc: List all listening TCP sockets with processes
commands.tooltip: lsof with -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN shows every open listening socket and the owning process; -P disables port-name lookups and -n disables hostname lookups for speed and accuracy. The output maps each open port to its process — the definitive answer to 'what is running on port X'. Compare with ss -tlnp, which shows the same picture differently.

commands.desc: Edit a sudo drop-in file safely
commands.tooltip: visudo validates syntax before saving — the -f flag points it at a drop-in file in /etc/sudoers.d/, the clean way to grant the deploy user specific sudo rights (like a no-password restart of myapp) without touching the main sudoers file. A broken sudoers file can lock everyone out of sudo, which is exactly what visudo prevents.
